Q: Retrieving datetime vales from database and converting to UNIX time A:

First of all, creating a UNIX timestamp is NOT needed for server to server communication, as all languages and databases have date types. XML and JSON also support date literals in ISO8601 form. If, as the comments say, the source and target systems are SQL Server with a Web API in front of the target, the easiest way is to just use a datetimeoffset field in the DTO.

Second, this is very much a timezone issue. The database right now stores a local time in an unknown timezone. To convert that to UTC, the timezone must be known. If the server, all clients and all stored values (past and future) are in the same timezone, that conversion is easy.

What the question's code does is equivalent to callling SQL Server's AT TIME ZONE to convert the local value to a datetimeoffset and then to UTC, eg :

select getdate() at TIME ZONE 'Cen. Australia Standard Time' AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'

Using an offset alone isn't enough, as due to DST rules, it can change. Even DST rules themselves can change.

If the application only stores past dates, you could get away with always storing UTC times. Future dates will break if DST rules change. Russia changed DST rules at least 3 times within a short period, Egypt changed them with something like 6 months warning. Even if you only store past dates, you'll have to ensure that all client applications convert to UTC when storing dates.

Somewhat similar is changing the column type to datetimeoffset(0) and changing the code to use DateTimeOffset. That still doesn't handle future DST rule changes, but at least the code changes are easier and any mistakes will result in errors that can be fixed.

The option that handles everything is to store local time and the timezone name. This way, no matter how rules change, you can convert to the correct time at any point. You can also mix different timezones. This is explained in Jon Skeet's Storing UTC is not a silver bullet

This example stores times for different timezones in the same table, and won't be affected by changes.

declare @departures table(
    Flight nvarchar(20),
    Departure datetime2(0),
    Airport_TZ nvarchar(50)
)

insert into @departures (Flight,Departure,Airport_TZ)
values
('AA111','2027-03-01 03:00','Cen. Australia Standard Time'),
('AB111','2027-06-01 03:00','W. Europe Standard Time')

select * ,Departure at time zone Airport_TZ AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' as UTC
from @departures
-----

Flight  Departure   Airport_TZ                          UTC
AA111   2027-03-01 03:00:00 Cen. Australia Standard Time    2027-02-28 16:30:00 +00:00
AB111   2027-06-01 03:00:00 W. Europe Standard Time         2027-06-01 01:00:00 +00:00

You can convert the UTC expression into a computed column too, avoiding conversions in code:

declare @departures table(
    Flight nvarchar(20),
    Departure datetime2(0),
    Airport_TZ nvarchar(50),
    UTC AS Departure at time zone Airport_TZ AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'
)

...
select * from @departures

CAVEAT: Windows timezone names are ... not used by anyone except Windows and SQL Server. If you complain that they can shift ... you'd be right. What everyone else uses is the IANA Timezone database, which uses TZ names like Europe/Oslo or Australia/Adelaide, Australia/Sydney. Even on Linux, SQL Server will map IANA names to Windows timezone names

Every other database uses IANA timezone names.

Q: Are a const std::vector<T>'s elements logical or physical const? A:

The objects held by a const std::vector<T> are non-const (assuming T is non-const; I actually can't remember whether T is allowed to be const). This follows from the fact that a constructor can't tell whether it's constructing a const object; since a std::vector<T> initialized to hold some Ts will construct non-const Ts into the buffer it owns, the same constructor call must do exactly the same thing when called for a const vector.

The actual specification is implied by the requirements on T for sequence containers and for std::vector specifically, e.g., for the OP's example of construction from an initializer list, [sequence.reqmts]/8 applies: T must be Cpp17EmplaceConstructible. According to [container.alloc.reqmts]/2.5, this means the expression allocator_traits<A>::construct(m, p, args) is well-formed, where p is of type T*. That means an object of the pointed-to type, T, will be constructed (as implied by the specification of allocator_traits and the Cpp17Allocator requirements).

Q: Firefox PDF previewer assign Firefox tab title, as PDF's meta title and PDF's file name, how change A:

Not currently, AFAIK, but it's not a bad idea. Lots of PDF titles start with "Microsoft Word...", which is less descriptive in the available space than the filename.

Options that PDF.js takes from about:config are defined here:
https://github.com/mozilla/pdf.js/blob/0c8f67059e1d0e06291b85a38860ae5d3723a402/web/app_options.js

There is no search match for "title" so presumably, no such option currently exists.

The page's document.title property (seen in tab name) is set here:
https://github.com/mozilla/pdf.js/blob/0c8f67059e1d0e06291b85a38860ae5d3723a402/web/app.js#L1851

The line linked contains a check whether the metadata of the document contain a title that can be shown. You can add a check for a new option you define in app_options.js, and then submit a pull request for this. If accepted, there will be an about:config value such as pdfjs.ignorePdfTitle that accomplishes this. Don't forget to set the default value to what people are currently used to.
It would be good practice to simultaneously submit an equivalent patch for the mobile version of PDF.js too, see lines 135-174 here https://github.com/mozilla/pdf.js/blob/0c8f67059e1d0e06291b85a38860ae5d3723a402/examples/mobile-viewer/viewer.mjs#L135

Alternatively, you can try making a userscript, PDF.js has some API available that might allow you to run code after the document is parsed, I haven't looked into that.
